processing: As with other Mengku raw pu-erh, the leaf is pan-fired, rolled and sun-dried, then pressed or kept loose, with no ripening pile.
harvest_season: Spring is the most valued picking, as is usual across Mengku.
appearance_dry: Long dark green strips of large leaf, typical of Mengku raw tea.
appearance_wet: Thick yellow-green large leaves that open fully.
taste_profile: Little is recorded about this village's own taste. As with other Mengku raw teas, expect a full body, some bitterness and a returning sweetness.

brewing.notes: Treat it like other strong young Mengku tea: hot water, short early steeps, and longer ones only once the bitterness has settled.

vintage_note: Sold by harvest year as loose mao cha or pressed cakes, and often simply as part of the Bingdao name. One spring price list gave 1,300 to 1,500 yuan a kilo for small and medium trees and 2,200 to 2,500 for old trees, so far below the old village. Check that a 'Bingdao' label says which of the five villages it means.
description:
Dijie is one of the five settlements of the Bingdao village committee in Mengku, on the western side of the Nanmeng River alongside the old village and Nanpo. It is a way to drink within the Bingdao name at a fraction of the old village's price.

The method is standard for raw pu-erh here, and the character comes from Mengku large-leaf trees. Little is written about Dijie's own process or flavour, so anything finer than the Mengku norm should be taken from the tea in front of you.

As with other Mengku raw teas, expect a thick body, some bitterness and returning sweetness. Brew with hot water and short steeps, then compare it against a cup of Bingdao old village to find out what the price gap buys.

The old garden is small, with an annual pick of fresh leaf in the region of a thousand kilos, and it goes to merchants from the Bingdao villages. That makes pure Dijie old-tree tea hard to pin down, and a label saying only 'Bingdao' tells you little.
history: Dijie's old village once had about 60 households. In 2004 Shuangjiang County moved the whole village down to the highway because the site was remote and close to forest, but by 2007 more than ten Lahu families had moved back. About 50 to 60 acres of old gardens remain there.
